content.title: Planning and Strategic Instruments
content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition

content.text: Lesson 1 Overview

This lesson introduces key national instruments used to plan and implement sustainable energy transitions, including long-term strategies, national energy policies, and sectoral action plans. It examines how countries set energy and climate goals, align them with development priorities, and operationalize them through tools like renewable energy plans, efficiency strategies, and <ai prompt="Tell me more about clean cooking.">clean cooking 💬️</ai> roadmaps.

content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition
content.title: A: National Energy and Climate Strategies

content.text:
The global climate crisis is, at its core, an energy crisis.

Over 70% of global greenhouse gas emissions originate from the production, transformation, and consumption of energy, primarily from fossil fuel sources such as coal, oil, and natural gas. As scientific consensus on the urgency of limiting global warming strengthens, it has become increasingly evident that achieving international climate goals depends fundamentally on transforming the global energy system.

The development of international climate policy has followed a trajectory of expanding scope and ambition.

While early frameworks focused primarily on emissions reduction, later agreements more explicitly embedded energy transition objectives within global climate governance.
nationally determined contributions 💬️ (NDCs)

NDCs are the core planning instruments through which Parties to the Paris Agreement communicate their climate ambitions. As both policy declarations and strategic frameworks, NDCs serve to operationalize the global temperature goals established under Articles 2 and 4 of the Agreement.

While mitigation targets and sectoral emissions reductions remain central to NDCs, the energy sector occupies a particularly prominent role.

Given that energy systems account for over 70 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, the transition from fossil fuels to sustainable, sufficient, and efficient renewable-based energy systems is not only a technical requirement, but a structural prerequisite for meeting the objectives of the Paris Agreement.

content.title: BOX: The Paris Agreement And NDCs

content.text:
The Paris Agreement, adopted in 2015 under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), marks a turning point in the integration of energy policy into global climate governance. While prior international frameworks treated energy transition as an indirect outcome of mitigation efforts, the Paris Agreement places it at the center of implementation.

Its long-term temperature goals, aiming to keep global warming well below 2°C and ideally to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, inherently necessitate a substantial reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, the primary source of which is the combustion of fossil fuels for energy. Achieving these ambitious temperature targets requires a fundamental shift towards cleaner energy sources.
The Global Stocktake (GST)

GST is a key accountability mechanism established under Article 14 of the Paris Agreement. Occurring every five years, it assesses the collective progress of all countries toward achieving the Agreement’s long-term goals, particularly those related to mitigation, adaptation, and means of implementation, including finance, technology, and capacity-building.

The first Global Stocktake concluded in 2023 and provided critical insights into the global state of climate ambition. Among its most striking findings was the persistent gap between current nationally determined contributions (NDCs) and the emissions pathways consistent with limiting global warming to 1.5°C: It emphasized that without a rapid acceleration in clean energy deployment and a corresponding decline in fossil fuel use, the Paris temperature goals will remain out of reach.
The Ratchet mechanism”?

NDCs are meant to be updated over time. A key principle of the Paris Agreement is that countries would “ratchet up” their plans – that is, increase their efforts every five years to reflect their “highest possible ambition” of each Party. Ultimately, these revised and updated NDCs would mark stepping-stones on a pathway towards net-zero by 2050.
The first generation of NDCs were part of the initial adoption of the Paris Agreement in 2015. The second generation represents the initial update, which was due in 2020.

We already see the ratchet mechanism working. The first generation of NDCs reflected an aggregate reduction in the average global temperature target to 3.7 degrees Celsius. In contrast, the second generation of NDCs brought this down to 2.7 degrees Celsius. Although it is not enough to fully meet the goals outlined in the Paris Agreement, it signifies a step in the right direction.

According to the 2023 UNEP Production Gap Report, governments are projected to produce 110 percent more fossil fuels in 2030 than would be consistent with a 1.5°C pathway, and 69 percent more than would align with a 2°C trajectory.

By 2050, the production gap is expected to reach 350 percent and 150 percent, respectively. Without mechanisms to manage the equity implications of transitioning away from fossil fuels, including employment displacement and affordability challenges, these climate and energy targets are unlikely to be achieved at the necessary scale or pace.

Despite this, the integration of just energy transition 💬️ principles into NDCs remains underdeveloped and inconsistent.

Only 40 percent of current NDCs contain any reference to just transition. Of these, merely 17 percent include a dedicated section addressing the social, economic, and distributive dimensions of energy transitions. The proportion of such NDCs is even lower among developing countries, where the risks of social disruption, energy poverty, and exclusion are often more acute.

Furthermore, the UNFCCC’s 2023 synthesis report found that only 31 percent of Parties explicitly address the unequal impacts of climate measures on workers and vulnerable groups.
Long-Term Climate Strategies

They can help evaluate and demonstrate socio-economic benefits. For example, Chile’s LTS showed that moving towards carbon neutrality 💬️ by 2050 could lead to direct economic savings of more than US$267 billion, just considering energy targets. Such evaluations help decision makers to justify climate-friendly public policies, including those with strong social benefits, such as improved health outcomes, expanded energy access, job security, and enhanced resilience.

They can help strengthen and guide NDCs. An LTS provides a long-term vision that gives coherence and direction to shorter-term national climate pledges like Nationally Determined Contributions, or NDCs. The LTS allows a country to link short-term development planning (including its NDC) to its long-term objectives, providing a framework for policy development.

They help prevent fossil fuel-intensive investments. When a country articulates its LTS, it facilitates discussions on climate ambition and possible policy responses. This might include emphasis on preventing investments in fossil fuel-intensive systems that delay or obstruct the transition to low-carbon alternatives – which would put the country’s climate efforts in danger and potentially causing higher costs for transition to a low-carbon economy.

They send clear economic signals. LTS give early and predictable market signals to investors around technological trends and long-term growth plans. In turn, a country is able to make more efficient decisions without regret around public and private investments and guide public discussion on ways to achieve low-carbon development.

They can facilitate a just transition. When a country has a clear plan for becoming sustainable, it has to consider the needs of all people who might be most affected, including those who are already struggling. This is called a "just transition" and it helps make sure no one is left behind. LTS can provide clear guidance on how to manage the transition in a fair and inclusive manner.

They can facilitate climate financing. LTS allow countries a chance to adequately plan budgeting mechanisms to finance de-carbonized development pathways. This includes facilitating access to international climate financing, which is growing increasingly important.

They can facilitate institutional strengthening. The cross-cutting nature of LTS requires public policies and fiscal incentives to be well-aligned, with buy-in from key ministries. Therefore, long-term climate planning encourages coordination between sectors and at all levels of government to develop, incentivize, implement, and monitor key climate actions.

The Four Pillars of Integrating Just Transition into Climate Planning

Recognizing the social, economic, and political risks posed by uncoordinated decarbonization 💬️, the UNDP has developed a four-pillar framework for integrating just transition principles into NDCs and LTS.

This framework, comprising Assessment, Engagement, Institutional and Policy Support, and Finance, responds to the growing need to align national climate targets with inclusive, rights-based, and development-oriented energy transitions.
Engagement

Social dialogue and inclusive participation are core to building legitimacy and reducing resistance to energy transition reforms. The engagement pillar focuses on structured consultations with key stakeholders, including trade unions, employer associations, women’s groups, Indigenous Peoples, youth networks, and subnational governments. In South Africa, for example, the National Economic Development and Labour Council (NEDLAC) facilitates tri-partite dialogue among government, labor, and business to shape national just transition policy. In Antigua and Barbuda, consultations were initiated with worker representatives and sectoral actors on climate-resilient development.
Assessment

Effective just transition planning begins with systematic assessment. UNDP supports countries in conducting qualitative and quantitative transition assessments, using tools such as employment modeling, macroeconomic forecasting, and green jobs diagnostics. These assessments estimate the impacts of decarbonization measures on employment, income distribution, skills needs, gender equity, and vulnerable populations. For instance, renewable energy investment in Nigeria showed job creation potential of 150 jobs per $1 million.
Assessment

The third pillar addresses the structural and regulatory conditions necessary to implement just transition measures at scale. It includes the development of long-term transition roadmaps, regulatory frameworks for labor protection, integration of just transition language into national development plans, and the creation of monitoring and accountability mechanisms. For example, Armenia is in the process of developing a national framework for a low-carbon, socially inclusive economy. In Colombia, UNDP supported the design of just transition recommendations within the country’s 2050 strategy, explicitly linking energy, agriculture, and transport sector policies to labor market outcomes and consumer behavior.

National Energy Policy (NEP)

National Energy Policies (NEPs) serve as a country’s overarching framework for guiding the production, distribution, and consumption of energy. While policies differ in scope and ambition across countries, most NEPs are designed to address three core objectives,energy security, affordability, and environmental sustainability,often referred to as the energy trilemma.

At their core, NEPs define national priorities across the energy value chain 💬️. This includes decisions on the energy mix (e.g., share of renewables, fossil fuels, nuclear), targets for energy access and efficiency, and policies to attract investment in infrastructure. In the context of climate change and the global push for decarbonization, many NEPs now also embed climate mitigation goals aligned with NDCs and LTSs.
India
Rwanda

As seen, NEPs differ by country context, common components include:

Vision and Targets: Long-term energy goals (e.g., net-zero emissions by 2050, 100% electricity access by 2030)
Energy Demand and Supply Projections: Forecasts across sectors and scenarios
Resource Allocation and Technology Mix: Prioritization of energy sources and technologies
Cross-Cutting Issues: Gender, climate adaptation, finance, decentralization, and job creation
Legal, Institutional, and Regulatory Frameworks: Roles of government, utilities, and private sector

content.title: Case Study: Barbados
content.subtitle: Barbados National Energy Policy (BNEP) 2019–2030: Building a Just and Renewable Energy Future

content.text:
Barbados long struggled with an imported energy trap. With no domestic oil or gas, the island relied on diesel and heavy fuel oil for over 90 percent of its electricity generation. By the early 2010s, Barbados had some of the world’s highest electricity tariffs, while volatile global oil prices repeatedly strained the economy, and foreign exchange reserves fuel imports consumed roughly 5 percent of GDP. Low-income families, businesses, and public services all felt the pinch. Energy policy had been fragmented, and energy sovereignty was virtually non-existent. Climate risks loomed large, but local institutions and financial resources were limited, creating systemic barriers to change.
It was against this backdrop that Barbados set out to transform its energy sector.
In 2019, Barbados launched its National Energy Policy (BNEP) 2019–2030, a bold roadmap to break fossil-fuel dependency (Government of Barbados, 2019). The policy’s centerpiece was its goal to become a 100 percent renewable, carbon-neutral island by 2030. Under the vision of ‘energy security and affordability through diversity and collaboration,’ the BNEP is committed to reliable, affordable, and climate-friendly power for all. Key targets included zero domestic fossil-fuel use, minimized foreign exchange outflows, and increased local participation in distributed energy generation (referred to in the policy as the ‘democratization of energy’) (Government of Barbados, 2019, p. 14, para. 1-2). Any hydrocarbon resources found offshore were designated for export only, turning fossil resources into a financial asset for sustainable development (Government of Barbados, 2019, pp. 14, 30).

This vision was built on more than a decade of reforms. Barbados had already introduced net metering, launched a national solar water heating program, and operated a Smart Energy Fund that supports solar PV and energy efficiency projects. These efforts were consolidated into a cohesive framework during extensive multi-stakeholder consultations between 2016 and 2018. The BNEP outlined legal and institutional reforms, financial strategies, and equity goals, including gender-sensitive approaches. It revised the Electric Light and Power Act, introduced feed-in tariffs for solar producers, expanded public-private partnerships 💬️, and integrated renewable energy into national planning frameworks.
In 2024, Barbados published an official implementation plan to translate policy into action. The plan was shaped by participatory processes involving ministries, utilities, financiers, NGOs, and citizen groups. A high-level Resource Coordination Team (RCT), co-chaired by the Ministries of Energy and Finance, was established to manage inter-agency coordination, align with national climate goals, and mobilize the estimated BBD 4 billion needed to implement the transition.
The implementation plan operationalized the BNEP through four thematic working groups: renewable energy transport, electricity and efficiency, oil and gas, and environment and climate change. Public sector retrofits, regulatory reforms, and communication campaigns were prioritized. The BREA and other civil society actors played a central role in mainstreaming gender and inclusion in the implementation process. The plan also introduced a change-management approach (ADKAR model) and a robust monitoring and evaluation framework, including quarterly reviews, annual reports, and a digital transparency platform (Government of Barbados, 2024).

Results followed quickly. By 2022, Barbados had installed approximately 70 MW of solar PV capacity, more than doubling its 2019 level. The St. Lucy Solar Park (10 MW), commissioned in 2016, generates around 20 GWh annually, powering 7,700 homes and offsetting more than 21,000 metric tons of CO₂ emissions per year (Caribbean Centre for Renewable Energy & energy efficiency 💬️, 2024; GlobalData/Power‑Technology, 2024).
Public-sector investments expanded significantly under Barbados’s Smart Energy Programme. The government retrofitted approximately 85% of public streetlights with energy-efficient technologies and installed solar photovoltaic (PV) systems on multiple public buildings, including schools and hospitals (GIS Barbados, 2023). Notably, the Samuel Jackman Prescod Institute of Technology (SJPI) hosts a 109-kW solar PV system, which generates over 200,000 kWh annually and saves an estimated BBD 85,000 each year. This system also serves as a practical training facility for students in renewable energy technologies (GIS Barbados, 2023). In the transportation sector, the Barbados Transport Board has incorporated electric buses into its fleet, totaling 59 electric buses as of mid-2023 (Government of Barbados, 2023). Additionally, the government has incentivized the adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) by reducing import duties and VAT on EVs and hybrids while also supporting the development of charging infrastructure. These initiatives have contributed to a growing share of electric vehicles among private imports, reflecting increased public confidence and supportive policy frameworks (Central Bank of Barbados, 2023).

These reforms are yielding substantial economic and social benefits. Government projections suggest that eliminating fossil fuel imports could yield a socio-economic benefit of BBD 2.2 billion annually (Government of Barbados, 2017). Fossil fuel use for electricity generation dropped below 91 percent in 2022, down from over 99 percent a decade prior. In parallel, new industries and jobs are emerging in solar installation, maintenance, and clean energy entrepreneurship (EBSCO Research Starters, 2024).

Barbados’s experience offers valuable lessons for small island developing states 💬️ and low-income countries facing similar energy and climate challenges. These lessons are as follows:
First, effective political leadership, clear policy, and a long-term vision are essential. Setting a clear 2030 target mobilized public and private actors around a shared goal.
Second, institutions matter. Barbados established a cross-sectoral governance structure, spanning from Cabinet to community, supported by legal reforms and regular dialogue.
Third, securing financing early from multilateral funds, donors, and private investors enabled scaling.
Fourth, investing in transparency and inclusivity built trust, predominantly when implementation was guided by gender-sensitive engagement and continuous stakeholder feedback.
Crucially, Barbados recognized its strengths, abundant sunshine, an educated youth, and a tourism-driven economy, and tailored solutions accordingly. By aligning energy policy with economic development, the BNEP turned a national vulnerability into a strategic asset.

content.intro: M5: Energy Governance for a Just Energy Transition
content.title: B: Sectoral and Thematic Action Plans

content.text: While high-level policies such as NEP and LTSs) define overarching energy and climate goals, their implementation depends on targeted sectoral and thematic action plans. These plans translate strategic intent into measurable outcomes through concrete interventions tailored to specific sectors such as renewable energy, energy efficiency, transport, and clean cooking. This section highlights four key types of action plans that serve as critical instruments for delivering national and international climate commitments.
National Energy Efficiency Action Plans (NEEAPs)
National Renewable Energy Action Plans (NREAPs)

NEEAPs outline sector-specific interventions to reduce energy intensity and optimize energy use across residential, commercial, industrial, and transport sectors. Common features include the introduction of Minimum Energy Performance Standards (MEPS), market-based incentives, and public awareness campaigns. NEEAPs also prioritize institutional reforms,such as the creation of Energy Efficiency Units and dedicated oversight committees,to support effective implementation. These plans function as both technical roadmaps and governance tools and promotes regulatory clarity, stakeholder engagement, and long-term energy savings.

NREAPs function as core planning documents that define a country’s medium-term approach to scaling up renewable energy. Their primary purpose is to operationalize the national energy strategy or climate commitments,such as those articulated in Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs),by establishing renewable energy targets, identifying priority technologies, and detailing enabling policy and financial measures. These plans often span a 10- to 15-year horizon and provide sector-specific implementation pathways for hydropower, wind, solar, geothermal, and <ai prompt="Explain bioenergy.">bioenergy 💬️</ai>. Effective NREAPs go beyond setting targets. They provide legal, regulatory, and institutional frameworks to support project development, facilitate grid integration, promote distributed energy access, and attract private investment.
Clean Cooking Action Plans and Strategies

Clean Cooking Action Plans are comprehensive strategies aimed at accelerating the transition to modern cooking solutions and reducing reliance on polluting fuels like wood, charcoal, and kerosene. These plans define national goals for access to clean fuels and technologies, identify priority interventions, and establish mechanisms for behavioral change, financing, and market development. Clean cooking action plans address energy poverty, health risks from indoor air pollution, and gender disparities by promoting solutions that are affordable, culturally appropriate, and environmentally sustainable. Their design and implementation require coordination between energy, health, environment, and gender ministries, and must be underpinned by supportive regulatory frameworks, targeted subsidies, and public awareness campaigns.

electric mobility 💬️ roadmaps are strategic planning tools that set timelines and targets for electric vehicle (EV) adoption while guiding infrastructure development and local industry support. These plans typically combine demand-side measures (e.g., EV purchase subsidies, import duty exemptions) with supply-side enablers (e.g., public charging infrastructure, local battery production).
